'''John Harding Lucas II''' (born October 31, 1953) is an American professional [[basketball]] coach and former player who most recently served as an assistant coach for the [[Houston Rockets]] of the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA). He played basketball and [[tennis]] at the [[University of Maryland, College Park]] and was an [[All-American]] in both.

==Collegiate career==
Lucas attended the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]] where he was an All-American in basketball. Lucas was a Second-team All-American for the Terrapins team in 1973–74, along with his teammates [[Len Elmore]] and [[Tom McMillen]]. The Terrapins had a record of 23–5 in the regular season, and 9–3 in the [[Atlantic Coast Conference]] (ACC). However, they lost during the ACC Tournament, and they could not go to the NCAA Tournament. Elmore and McMillan graduated in 1974, but in the following 1974–75 season, Lucas was a First-team All-American. The Terrapins recorded a 24–5 regular season record, 10–2 in the ACC, and they won the ACC regular season crown. However, they lost to NC State in the semifinals of the ACC tournament. The NCAA tournament, however, had been expanded to include 32 teams. Also, for the first time, more than one team per conference was allowed into the tournament. Maryland gained entry and advanced to the Elite Eight before losing to Louisville.

Lucas played for the [[United States men's national basketball team|US national team]] in the [[1974 FIBA World Championship]], winning the bronze medal.<ref>[http://www.usabasketball.com/news.php?news_page=mwc_1974 SEVENTH WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP -- 1974] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100103175822/http://usabasketball.com/news.php?news_page=mwc_1974 |date=January 3, 2010 }}</ref>

In the 1975–76 season, Lucas was a First-team All-American once again. The Terrapins recorded a 22–6 regular season record, 7–5 in the ACC, but they lost out in the ACC Tournament and did not make the NCAA Tournament.

==Professional career==

Lucas was the first overall pick of the [[1976 NBA draft]], selected by the [[Houston Rockets]].  He was also drafted by the [[New York Nets]] of the [[American Basketball Association]].<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20110520174408/http://databasebasketball.com/teams/teamyear.htm?tm=NYN&lg=a&yr=1975 1975 New York Nets draft page at DatabaseBasketball.com]}}</ref>

Lucas played in the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] for fourteen years. Lucas initially played for the Rockets for two years before NBA commissioner [[Larry O'Brien]] awarded him to the Golden State Warriors as compensation for the Rockets signing [[Rick Barry]] as a free agent.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Blinebury |first1=Fran |title='This city saved my life' -- John Lucas on his return to Houston, NBA |url=https://www.nba.com/news/john-lucas-houston-rockets-return-nba |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=www.nba.com |date=2016-11-01 |language=en}}</ref> While a member of the [[Golden State Warriors]], on October 20, 1978, Lucas scored a career-best 35 points during a 111–108 win over the Trail Blazers.<ref>{{cite web |title=John Lucas II Career High 35 Points |url=https://www.statmuse.com/nba/ask/john-lucas-ii-career-high-points-statmuse |website=Statmuse}}</ref> In his last season with the Warriors, Lucas's problems began when he missed a series of practice sessions, plane trips and games.<ref name="johnson1">{{cite news |last1=Johnson |first1=Roy S. |title=JOHN LUCAS TRIES TO RECAST HIS IMAGE |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/05/05/sports/john-lucas-tries-to-recast-his-image.html |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=The New York Times |date=5 May 1982}}</ref><ref name="mccallum">{{cite news |last1=McCallum |first1=Jack |title=JOHN LUCAS: PICKING UP THE PIECES |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1981/06/08/john-lucas-picking-up-the-pieces-the-mysterious-behavior-of-golden-states-point-guard-last-season-raised-many-questions-after-therapy-lucas-offers-answers |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=Sports Illustrated Vault {{!}} SI.com |language=en-us}}</ref> The Warriors suspended Lucas and chose not to pick up his contract option.<ref name="mccallum" />

After signing with the [[Washington Wizards|Washington Bullets]] as a free agent, Lucas continued to miss practices with the Bullets. He admitted that he was addicted to cocaine at the beginning of the 1982–1983 season and entered a rehabilitation program.<ref name="johnson1" /> The Bullets waived him in 1983.<ref>{{cite news  |title=JOHN LUCAS : This Ex-Maryland Star Survived Drug Addiction, but Not Without Problems |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-11-23-sp-12376-story.html |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=23 November 1986}}</ref>

Lucas played professional tennis and minor league basketball before returning to the NBA with the San Antonio Spurs and then moving on to Houston.<ref name="feinstein">{{cite news |last1=Feinstein |first1=John |title=JOHN LUCAS : This Ex-Maryland Star Survived Drug Addiction, but Not Without Problems |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1986-11-23-sp-12376-story.html |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=23 November 1986}}</ref> Lucas's drug problems continued to plague him, and the Rockets waived him in 1984 and reinstated him the next season after he underwent rehabilitation.<ref name="feinstein" /><ref name="newman">{{cite news |last1=Newman |first1=Bruce |title=THREE STRIKES AND HE'S...BACK |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1987/03/02/three-strikes-and-hesback |access-date=8 June 2022 |work=Sports Illustrated Vault {{!}} SI.com |date=1987-03-02 |language=en-us}}</ref> Lucas became a regular season starter for the [[1985–86 NBA season|1986]] [[Houston Rockets]]. However, after failing two drug tests, the Rockets waived Lucas in March before they embarked on a playoff run to the [[1986 NBA Finals]].<ref name="newman" />

Lucas was given another chance in January 1987 when he was signed to a ten-day contract by the Milwaukee Bucks that led to a full contract for the rest of the season.<ref>{{Cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/01/15/sports/rockets-discuss-drug-temptation.html | title=Rockets Discuss Drug Temptation| newspaper=The New York Times| date=January 15, 1987| last1=Johnson| first1=Roy S.}}</ref> Lucas played four more years in the NBA, averaging at age 33 a career-high 17.5 points for Milwaukee in 1986–87, after which, on May 8, 1987, he scored a team high 30 points to lead the Bucks to an Eastern Conference Semifinals Game 3 win over the Boston Celtics.<ref>{{cite web |title=1987 NBA Eastern Conference Semifinals Game 3: Boston Celtics at Milwaukee Bucks |url=https://www.basketball-reference.com/boxscores/198705080MIL.html |website=Basketball Reference}}</ref> The Bucks would go on to lose the series in seven games. Lucas played more of a reserve role for the next three years.

Lucas played three games with the [[Wichita Falls Texans]] in the [[Continental Basketball Association]] (CBA) during the 1991–92 season.<ref name=sc>{{cite web |title=John Lucas minor league basketball statistics |url=https://www.statscrew.com/minorbasketball/stats/p-lucasjoh002 |website=Stats Crew |access-date=October 26, 2023}}</ref> He was serving as head coach of the Miami Tropics in the [[United States Basketball League]] (USBL) at the time and appeared to help his player, [[Roy Tarpley]], who was scared about making his debut after leaving a drug treatment facility.<ref name=os />

After successfully undergoing drug rehabilitation and starting programs of his own to help other athletes rehabilitate, Lucas returned to the NBA as a coach, eventually becoming a head coach.

Lucas runs a wellness and aftercare substance-abuse recovery program for athletes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/24383926/jackie-macmullan-ocd-adhd-medication-marijuana-nba-mental-health|access-date=7 June 2019|title=How OCD almost ended one NBA player's career before it began|date=August 22, 2018}}</ref> Lucas has helped multiple professional athletes with substance abuse, including [[Freeman Williams]], with whom he became close friends.<ref>[https://www.oregonlive.com/vikings/2022/05/former-portland-state-great-freeman-williams-was-more-than-just-a-vikings-legend-he-was-an-icon.html Placing Portland State basketball legend Freeman Williams’ career in proper perspective: ‘He was an icon’]</ref>

==Coaching career==
On August 8, 1991, Lucas bought the Miami Tropics franchise of the [[United States Basketball League]] to use the team as a tool in helping players overcome drug problems.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Moore |first1=Toni |title=Lucas has rehab plans for USBL Tropics |url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1991/08/09/lucas-has-rehab-plans-for-usbl-tropics/ |website=Tampa Bay Times |access-date=October 26, 2023 |date=October 14, 2005}}</ref> He only intended to serve as team owner but realised he would be best suited as head coach to help with counselling players.<ref name=os>{{cite web |title=TROPICS REDEFINE WORD 'REBOUND' |url=https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1992/06/29/tropics-redefine-word-rebound/ |website=Orlando Sentinel |access-date=October 26, 2023 |date=July 26, 2021}}</ref> Lucas won two championships in 1992 and 1993 before he decided to step aside.<ref>{{cite web |title=TROPICS REPEAT; LUCAS STEPS ASIDE |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/1993/07/07/tropics-repeat-lucas-steps-aside/ |website=South Florida Sun Sentinel |access-date=October 26, 2023 |date=September 25, 2021}}</ref>

He has coached the [[San Antonio Spurs]], [[Philadelphia 76ers]] and [[Cleveland Cavaliers]], each for less than two seasons, compiling a 174–258 overall coaching record. His most successful stint was with the Spurs.  In 1992–93, he took over from [[Jerry Tarkanian]] (9–11) and went 39–22 the rest of the season, and reached the Western Conference semi-finals.  The next year the Spurs finished 55–27 but lost in the first round of playoffs.

Prior to accepting the head coaching position for the Cavs, he was assistant coach for the [[Denver Nuggets]] for three seasons.

Lucas worked with Indiana Pacers guard [[T. J. Ford]] in Houston after the guard sustained a neck injury from a hard foul from [[Atlanta Hawks|Atlanta]]'s [[Al Horford]].<ref>[https://www.thestar.com/Sports/article/300460 Ford's biggest hurdle was all mental]</ref>

Lucas was hired for the 2009–10 NBA season as an assistant coach for the Los Angeles Clippers under head coach [[Mike Dunleavy, Sr.|Mike Dunleavy]].

Lucas began working with former NFL first-round pick [[JaMarcus Russell]] in 2010 as a life coach, but ceased this role in April 2011.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5618297|title = Sources: John Lucas advising ex-Raider Russell|date = September 26, 2010}}</ref>

In July 2016, Lucas joined the Houston Rockets as a player development coach.<ref>[http://www.chron.com/sports/rockets/article/John-Lucas-to-join-Rockets-organization-8332355.php John Lucas to join Rockets organization]</ref> On November 6, 2020, Lucas was announced as an assistant in the staff of new Rockets head coach [[Stephen Silas]].<ref>{{cite web |title=John Lucas joins Stephen Silas' staff with Houston Rockets |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/story/_/id/30262637/john-lucas-joins-stephen-silas-staff-houston-rockets-sources-say |website=ESPN |access-date=June 7, 2022 |date=November 6, 2020}}</ref>

==Tennis career==
Lucas was not only a standout basketball player, but also a standout [[tennis]] player. An All-American in the sport while at Maryland, he won ACC number one singles championship twice in 1974 and 1976, before being named the McKelvin Award winner as the conference's top all-around athlete. Lucas competed in two [[Grand Prix tennis]] tournaments in 1973, another in 1979, and a [[Challenger tennis|challenger]] event in 1979.  His best result was reaching the semi-finals of the challenger in [[Raleigh, North Carolina]], partnering [[Fred McNair]].  He won one other tour match, by default in doubles in 1973 in [[Merion, Pennsylvania]] while partnering [[Vic Seixas]].  He lost all four of the singles first round matches which he contested, and in straight sets.<ref>[http://www.atpworldtour.com/Tennis/Players/Lu/J/John-Lucas.aspx?t=pa&y=0&m=s&e=0 ATP.com]</ref>  His best singles result was a 4–6, 4–6 loss to [[John Austin (tennis)|John Austin]]. Lucas's career high ranking was 579th, in singles in December 1979.<ref>[http://www.atpworldtour.com/Tennis/Players/Lu/J/John-Lucas.aspx ATP profile page]</ref>  (Doubles computer rankings were not officially kept until the early 1980s.)

Lucas also played [[World Team Tennis]] with the [[San Francisco Golden Gaters]] in 1976, and the [[New Orleans Sun Belt Nets]] in 1978. He and [[Renée Richards]] had success teaming up as the Nets' regular mixed-doubles team in 1978. The 6'1" Richards was delighted to have a male partner who was taller than she was.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Richards|first1=Renée|last2=Ames|first2=John|year=2007|title=No Way Renée: The Second Half of My Notorious Life|location=New York|publisher=Simon & Schuster|isbn=978-0-7432-9013-5|lccn=2006052252|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/nowayreneesecond00rich}}</ref>

In 2005, Lucas was the head coach of the [[Houston Wranglers]], which featured [[Steffi Graf]] and [[Mardy Fish]].

==Personal life==
Lucas's elder son [[John Lucas III]] played college basketball at [[Oklahoma State University – Stillwater|Oklahoma State]] and has been a member of several NBA teams. His younger son, [[Jai Lucas|Jai]], is currently head coach at the University of Miami, was previously an assistant coach at [[Duke University]], and also played [[college basketball]] at the [[University of Texas]].
